The '''Mathematical Association''' is a professional society concerned with [[mathematics education]] in the United Kingdom.

==History==
It was founded in 1871 as the Association for the Improvement of Geometrical Teaching and renamed to the Mathematical Association in 1897.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Price |first1=Michael H |title=Mathematics for the Multitude?: A History of the Mathematical Association |date=1994 |publisher=The Mathematical Association |location=Leicester |isbn=0906588324 |page=41}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Moktefi |first1=Amirouche |editor1-last=Flood |editor1-first=Raymond |editor-link=Raymond Flood (mathematician) |editor2-last=Rice |editor2-first=Adrian |editor3-last=Wilson |editor3-first=Robin |editor3-link=Robin Wilson (mathematician) |title=Mathematics in Victorian Britain |date=2011 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |isbn=9780199601394 |page=333 |chapter=Geometry: The Euclid debate}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Furinghetti |first1=Fulvia |editor1-last=Karp |editor1-first=Alexander |editor2-last=Schubring |editor2-first=Gert |title=Handbook on the History of Mathematics Education |date=2014 |publisher=Springer |location=New York |isbn=978-1-4614-9154-5 |page=546 |chapter=History of International Cooperation in Mathematics Education}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fujita |first1=Taro |last2=Jones |first2=Keith |title=The Process of Redesigning the Geometry Curriculum: The Case of the Mathematical Association in England in the Early Twentieth Century |journal=The International Journal for the History of Mathematics Education |date=2011 |volume=6 |issue=1 |page=6}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Howson |first1=A.G. |title=Charles Godfrey (1873-1924) and the Reform of Mathematical Education |journal=Educational Studies in Mathematics |date=1973 |volume=5 |issue=2 |page=158}}</ref> It was the first teachers' subject organisation formed in England. In March 1927, it held a three-day meeting in [[Grantham]] to commemorate the bicentenary of the death of Sir [[Isaac Newton]], attended by Sir [[J. J. Thomson]] (discoverer of the electron), Sir [[Frank Watson Dyson]] – the [[Astronomer Royal]], Sir [[Horace Lamb]], and [[G. H. Hardy]].

In 1951, [[Mary Cartwright]] became the first female president of the Mathematical Association.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Williams | first = Mrs. E. M.| author-link = Elizabeth Williams (educationist)
 | date = October 1966
 | doi = 10.2307/3614669
 | issue = 373
 | pages = 243–254| journal = The Mathematical Gazette
 | title = Presidential Address: The Changing Role of Mathematics in Education
 | volume = 50| jstor = 3614669| s2cid = 186846165}}</ref>

In the 1960s, when comprehensive education was being introduced, the Association was in favour of the [[11-plus]] system. For maths teachers training at university, a teaching award that was examined was the [[Diploma of the Mathematical Association]], later known as the Diploma in Mathematical Education of the Mathematical Association.

==Function==
It exists to "bring about improvements in the teaching of mathematics and its applications, and to provide a means of communication among students and teachers of mathematics".<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.m-a.org.uk/association/organisation/ |title=The Mathematical Association – supporting mathematics in education<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=15 February 2008 |archive-date=13 March 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080313064255/http://www.m-a.org.uk/association/organisation/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Since 1894 it has published ''[[The Mathematical Gazette]]''. It is one of the participating bodies in the quadrennial British Congress of Mathematics Education, organised by the [[Joint Mathematical Council]], and it holds its annual general meeting as part of the Congress.<ref>[http://www.bcme.org.uk/write/MediaUploads/Handbook_Web_Version.pdf BMCE Handbook] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181010134908/https://www.bcme.org.uk/write/MediaUploads/Handbook_Web_Version.pdf |date=10 October 2018 }}, retrieved 2018-10-09</ref>

==Structure==
It is based in the south-east of Leicester on ''London Road'' ([[A6 road (England)|A6]]), just south of the Charles Frears campus of [[De Montfort University]].

Aside from the council, it has seven other specialist committees.

===Regions===
Its branches are sometimes shared with the [[Association of Teachers of Mathematics]] (ATM):
* Birmingham
* Cambridge
* East Midlands
* Exeter
* Gloucester
* Liverpool
* London 
* Greater Manchester
* Meridian
* Stoke and Staffordshire
* Sheffield
* Sussex
* Yorkshire
